title: Teaching & Mentoring
text:
I believe that the most meaningful measure of learning is whether students can apply fundamental principles to unfamiliar problems. My teaching emphasizes conceptual understanding, quantitative reasoning, experimental design, and independent problem-solving rather than memorization alone.
I combine step-by-step instruction with active learning, real-world research examples, and modern visualization tools. In bioengineering courses, I connect foundational concepts to authentic scientific challenges, such as designing molecular biosensors, interpreting cellular signaling dynamics, or evaluating engineered therapeutic systems.
My goal is for students to develop the confidence and intellectual independence to ask meaningful questions, critically evaluate evidence, and defend their scientific reasoning.

Research theme: Observe — live-cell molecular imaging and DNA repair

title: GLIDRE: Watching DNA Repair at Specific Genomic Loci
text:
The challenge
Traditional DNA damage assays provide valuable endpoints but have difficulty tracking the damage response at a defined, non-repetitive genomic locus in the same living cell over time. GLIDRE (Genomic Locus Imaging and DSB Repair Monitoring by Elastin-like Proteins) was developed to provide locus-specific visualization combined with a dynamic repair-associated readout.

title: GLIDRE: Watching DNA Repair at Specific Genomic Loci
section: Discovery 1 — Amplifying signals at non-repetitive genomic loci
text:
Discovery 1 — Amplifying signals at non-repetitive genomic loci



Figure 1. CRISPR-guided elastin-like protein assembly provides amplified locus-labeling signals in live cells. Source: uploaded GLIDRE manuscript, Figure 1.


Approach. Engineered dCas9–SunTag complexes recruit elastin-like protein assemblies to the genomic target. Condensate-associated signal amplification makes non-repetitive loci accessible to live-cell observation.
Key finding. The strategy provides an optical handle for following specified genomic sites and pairing locus tracking with induced DNA damage.

title: GLIDRE: Watching DNA Repair at Specific Genomic Loci
section: Discovery 2 — Measuring local DNA damage responses in real time
text:
Discovery 2 — Measuring local DNA damage responses in real time



Figures 2–3. Locus-targeted damage and 53BP1 recruitment dynamics, including representative time-lapse sequences. Source: uploaded GLIDRE manuscript.


Approach. Orthogonal AsCas12a induces DNA double-strand breaks near labeled loci, while recruitment and residence of the DNA damage response factor 53BP1 are monitored in living cells.
Key finding. GLIDRE supports time-resolved, locus-specific assessment of repair-associated dynamics. Importantly, 53BP1 residence is a proxy for the response rather than a direct measurement of completed repair.

title: GLIDRE: Watching DNA Repair at Specific Genomic Loci
section: Discovery 3 — Chromatin state influences repair-associated kinetics and therapy response
text:
Discovery 3 — Chromatin state influences repair-associated kinetics and therapy response



Figure 4. Chromatin accessibility, transcription perturbation, and repair-associated residence dynamics. Source: uploaded GLIDRE manuscript.





Figure 5. H3.3K27M-associated chromatin dysregulation, SAHA treatment, and CAR T-cell spheroid response. Source: uploaded GLIDRE manuscript.


Key finding. More accessible chromatin generally exhibited shorter 53BP1 residence than compacted chromatin, with transcription contributing in a context-dependent manner. In engineered H3.3K27M U2OS models, altered locus-specific dynamics accompanied reduced CAR T-cell response; SAHA treatment shifted the observed dynamics and increased spheroid sensitivity.

← All research highlights
Research theme: Engineer + Control — cis-activation and focused ultrasound
Publication: Molecular Therapy Oncology (2026) · Journal article

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
text:
The challenge
Tumor antigen heterogeneity and antigen escape limit durable CAR T-cell activity. CisCAR explores a different activation mechanism: engineering T cells to display the cognate antigen that activates their own CAR, then placing antigen expression under external thermal control.

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
section: Discovery 1 — CARs respond to antigen presented in cis
text:
Discovery 1 — CARs respond to antigen presented in cis



Figure 1. CisCAR construct design, receptor–antigen colocalization, and activation in Jurkat cells. Source: uploaded CisCAR Figure 1.


Approach. Cells coexpressing truncated CD19 and CD19 CAR were assessed for receptor colocalization and CD69 activation.
Key finding. Antigen presentation on the same cell promoted CAR-associated clustering and T-cell activation, supporting cis-activation as an engineered signaling mechanism.

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
section: Discovery 2 — Thermal control enables on-demand activation
text:
Discovery 2 — Thermal control enables on-demand activation



Figure 2. Heat-inducible tCD19 expression, time-lapse clustering, CD69, cytokines, and cell viability. Source: uploaded CisCAR Figure 2.


Approach. A heat-responsive promoter drives tCD19 expression, whereas the CAR is constitutively expressed. Localized heating serves as the trigger for self-activation.
Key finding. Induction promoted CD69 expression and inflammatory cytokine secretion in engineered T cells, while the investigated repeated-stimulation conditions did not show evidence of significant fratricide.

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
section: Discovery 3 — Activated CisCAR cells kill antigen-negative tumors
text:
Discovery 3 — Activated CisCAR cells kill antigen-negative tumors



Figure 3. Spatially limited bystander-killing concept and in vitro cytotoxicity experiments. Source: uploaded CisCAR Figure 3.


Approach. Thermal stimulation was applied to FUS-CisCAR cocultures containing antigen-negative tumor cells.
Key finding. Induced activation supported bystander killing of antigen-negative cells in the tested models, addressing an important dimension of tumor antigen escape.

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
section: Discovery 4 — Focused ultrasound enables local tumor control in vivo
text:
Discovery 4 — Focused ultrasound enables local tumor control in vivo



Figure 4. Mouse model, ultrasound treatment schedule, IVIS imaging, and tumor-response measurements. Source: uploaded CisCAR Figure 4.


Approach. FUS was applied to selected tumor sites in a bilateral mouse model after FUS-CisCAR delivery.
Key finding. Ultrasound-treated tumors showed improved local control compared with contralateral untreated sites in the reported experiment, supporting a strategy for spatially regulated antigen-independent cytotoxicity.

title: CisCAR: Ultrasound-Controlled T-Cell Self-Activation
text:
Why it matters
CisCAR links an unconventional engineered immune-cell activation mechanism to a noninvasive external trigger, offering a way to confine therapeutic activity to selected tissue regions even when tumor cells lack the canonical target antigen.

title: Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?
text:
Abstract
In a complete theory there is an element corresponding to each element of reality. A sufficient condition for the reality of a physical quantity is the possibility of predicting it with certainty, without disturbing the system. In quantum mechanics in the case of two physical quantities described by non-commuting operators, the knowledge of one precludes the knowledge of the other. Then either (1) the description of reality given by the wave function in quantum mechanics is not complete or (2) these two quantities cannot have simultaneous reality. Consideration of the problem of making predictions concerning a system on the basis of measurements made on another system that had previously interacted with it leads to the result that if (1) is false then (2) is also false. One is thus led to conclude that the description of reality as given by a wave function is not complete.

title: EchoRewire: Reprogramming Suppressive Signals for CAR T-Cell Therapy
text:
The challenge
The solid tumor microenvironment can suppress T-cell responses through factors such as TGF-β. Meanwhile, externally induced CAR expression can be transient. EchoRewire was developed to combine localized initiation with a microenvironment-driven mechanism for sustaining therapeutic activity.

title: EchoRewire: Reprogramming Suppressive Signals for CAR T-Cell Therapy
section: Discovery 1 — Redirecting TGF-β into stimulatory signals
text:
Discovery 1 — Redirecting TGF-β into stimulatory signals



Figure 1. Engineered TGF-β receptor rewirers and downstream NFκB signaling. Source: uploaded EchoRewire manuscript.


Approach. Chimeric receptors couple TGF-β-binding ectodomains to interleukin receptor signaling modules. The TG18 design redirects TGF-β stimulation toward the IL-18–MyD88–NFκB pathway.
Key finding. TG18 converts an inhibitory extracellular cue into pro-activation signaling, altering inflammatory and effector-associated responses in engineered T cells.

title: EchoRewire: Reprogramming Suppressive Signals for CAR T-Cell Therapy
text:
Discovery 2 — Building modular signaling options



Figure 2. Modular rewirer architectures and STAT pathway activity. Source: uploaded EchoRewire manuscript.


Approach. Rewirers with different intracellular domains were constructed to couple TGF-β input to alternative outputs, including STAT3 and STAT5 signaling.
Key finding. Signaling conversion can be programmed through receptor architecture rather than relying on a single output pathway.

title: EchoRewire: Reprogramming Suppressive Signals for CAR T-Cell Therapy
section: Discovery 3 — Integrating focused ultrasound and feedback
text:
Discovery 3 — Integrating focused ultrasound and feedback



Figure 3. Focused ultrasound initiation, rewirer-driven feedback, and antitumor activity. Source: uploaded EchoRewire manuscript.





Figure 4. Additional in vivo tumor response characterization. Source: uploaded EchoRewire manuscript.


Approach. FUS initiates localized CAR expression; rewirer-mediated TGF-β signaling then supports sustained activation through a positive feedback design.
Key finding. The integrated system demonstrated enhanced and more durable antitumor responses across the preclinical solid-tumor models tested.

title: EchoRewire: Reprogramming Suppressive Signals for CAR T-Cell Therapy
text:
Why it matters
EchoRewire treats the immunosuppressive tumor environment not only as a barrier but as a programmable input for therapeutic cells, while preserving a spatially targeted ultrasound initiation step.

title: PDbody: Engineering Tumor-Selective Molecular Recognition
text:
The challenge
PD-L1 is abundant in many tumors but also appears on healthy cells, creating risks for therapies that recognize PD-L1 indiscriminately. We asked whether a human-derived monobody scaffold could be engineered for preferential recognition under tumor-like acidic conditions and paired with an additional antigen-dependent safety gate.

title: PDbody: Engineering Tumor-Selective Molecular Recognition
text:
Discovery 1 — Developing a PD-L1-binding scaffold



Figure 1. Monobody scaffold, binding assays, and dependence on experimental pH conditions. Source: uploaded PDbody manuscript.


Approach. A human fibronectin type III-derived monobody scaffold was evaluated for PD-L1 recognition, including its pH-dependent binding behavior.
Key finding. Monobody–PD-L1 interaction was sensitive to assay conditions, motivating protein engineering aimed at binding under mildly acidic tumor-relevant conditions.

title: PDbody: Engineering Tumor-Selective Molecular Recognition
text:
Discovery 2 — Directed evolution improves recognition



Figure 2. Rational loop modification, library construction, and screening for improved PD-L1 recognition. Source: uploaded PDbody manuscript.


Approach. Rational design was combined with yeast display and successive directed-evolution libraries targeting monobody binding loops.
Key finding. The evolved PDbody provided a PD-L1-recognizing module suitable for integration into an engineered receptor system, with preferential binding under the lower-pH conditions evaluated.

title: PDbody: Engineering Tumor-Selective Molecular Recognition
section: Discovery 3 — Building a gated cellular therapy
text:
Discovery 3 — Building a gated cellular therapy



Figures 3–4. PDbody CAR testing and CD19-SynNotch-regulated PDbody CAR circuit. Source: uploaded PDbody manuscript.





Figure 5. Tumor control experiments in vivo. Source: uploaded PDbody manuscript.


Approach. A CD19-recognizing SynNotch circuit was used to induce PDbody-based CAR expression, requiring a priming antigen before PD-L1-directed effector activity.
Key finding. The engineered T cells achieved conditional recognition and antitumor activity in the investigated breast-cancer models, supporting combinatorial strategies to improve spatial specificity.

title: PDbody: Engineering Tumor-Selective Molecular Recognition
text:
Why it matters
PDbody illustrates a design-build-test approach spanning protein engineering, receptor design, and cellular therapy, with multiple layers of conditional recognition.
